7.9 Urinary and Reproductive Systems Impairment Evaluation Summary

Introduction

This chapter provides criteria for evaluating per-manent impairments of the genitorurinary system as they affect the body’s overall function and an individual’s ability to perform activities of daily living (ADLs). The entire chapter has been revised for the Sixth Edition of the AMA Guides using the rating system described in Chapter 1 to foster greater interrater reliability in the rating process. This includes a revision downward of the ratings for the highest classes of impairment, as many of these rat-ings reflected secondary impairment of other organ systems. In this edition of the Guides, readers are directed (unless specifically instructed otherwise) to rate secondary impairment separately and com-bine any ensuing rating with that for genitourinary impairment.

This edition of the Guides acknowledges that certain medications and treatments improve the overall physi-cal status of patients who receive them but result in some degree of impairment due to side effects or altera-tions in ADLs that result solely from their use. This has been described as the Burden of Treatment Compliance (BOTC) in other chapters. This is included in the rating

for disorders in this section, especially with regard to the use of dialysis. In addition, long-term use of high-dose steroids (in excess of 2 years on a daily basis) is generally associated with some adverse systemic effects and can be seen in some patients with renal failure. Refer to Chapter 10, Endocrine for additional details.

7.1 Principles of Assessment

Before using the information in this chapter, the Guides user should become familiar with Chapters 1 and 2 and the Glossary. Chapters 1 and 2 discuss the Guides’ purpose, applications, and methods for per-forming and reporting impairment evaluations. The Glossary provides definitions of common terms used by many specialties in impairment evaluations.

The purpose of assessment of genitourinary system impairment is to determine whether a permanent impairment in these systems exists, to assess the severity, and document the impact of the impairment on the ability to perform ADLs.

Pathologic abnormalities in other systems (eg, the hematologic, endocrine, or neurologic systems) may produce urinary or reproductive system impairment. These abnormalities are combined with urinary or reproductive system impairments to produce a whole person impairment rating. For example, renal dis-ease may lead to anemia that would be rated as part of hematopoietic impairment; an intracranial brain lesion above the pons will produce some degree of bladder hyperreflexia; an intracranial brain lesion below the pons will result not only in a hyperreflexic bladder but also in detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia (DSD). Some cases of dyssynergia may result in dif-ficulty urinating, high intravesical pressures, vesi-coureteral reflux, and subsequent hydronephrosis.1,2 Spinal cord injury patients with DSD will also have some degree of autonomic dysreflexia manifesting

with significant rise in blood pressure. This can be demonstrated during cystrometric examination and may need attention to prevent cardiovascular compli-cations.3 Urinary tract dysfunction is also seen with lumbosacral injury below the T10 vertebra level and would be combined with musculoskeletal impair-ment to determine whole person impairment.

To determine the individual’s placement in a particu-lar impairment class range, assess the history (symp-toms), physical findings, and results of objective tests. Assessment of functional level is not performed separately but is implicitly (and sometimes explic-itly) included as part of the rating. Considerations in the impairment rating include the degree to which disease affects functions specific to the urinary or reproductive system and overall function, as well as the impact of medication, regularly required proce-dures, and lifestyle modifications or interventions on the ability to perform general ADLs.

7.1a Methodology for Determining the Grade in an Impairment Class

This chapter employs impairment grids to use in determining the appropriate impairment class (class) and severity grade (grade) within a class for the con-dition or conditions being rated at Maximum Medical Improvement (MMI). As was stated in chapter 1, the decision regarding which factor is the primary deter-minant of impairment (key factor) will be clearly stated in each organ system impairment grid. The examiner will use this key factor to determine the appropriate class with the middle grade (integer) in that class as the initial (default) rating.

The examiner will then use non-key factors to assign grades for factors other than that considered “key,” with it being impossible to move upward or down-ward between classes based on these non-key factors. The number of potential grades for each impairment class varies based on the number of relevant factors.

When there are 2 non-key factors, there are generally 5 impairment grades per class; the presence of only one relevant factor other than the key factor reduces the number of possible grades to 3 per class.

If the examiner determines that the other factors affecting the rating are in the same class that had been used for the key factor rating, the final rating will generally stay in the middle of that class. On the other hand, if the classes chosen are higher or lower than that used for the baseline impairment rat-ing, the level will be moved to the right or to the left (to a higher or lower value) to reflect the numerical discrepancy. For example, if the key factor places the initial rating in class 3, grade C and there are 2 non-key factors (leading to a total of 5 possible grades) that are in class 1 and class 4, respectively, the first factor would move the grade down 2 levels to grade A and the second would move it back up 1 level to grade B. However, if both non-key factors were class 1, the rating could not go any lower than class 3, grade A, the lowest value for the class. An exception to this rule may occur when the key factor is in the highest impairment class for the disorder, as non-key factors falling in the same class can be used to adjust the impairment rating upward to the highest grade within the class rather than keep it at the middle level. Specific tables will indicate if a rating schema other than this is used.

The impairment criteria generally used in this chap-ter on the urinary and reproductive system include the history, physical findings, and objective test results. The assignment of a key factor and relative importance of the criteria will vary according to each regional disorder.

7.2 The Urinary System

The urinary system consists of the upper urinary tract (the kidneys and ureters), the bladder, and the urethra. The parenchyma of the kidneys produces urine, which is conducted through the renal calices, pelvis, ureters, bladder, and then the urethra.

The kidneys are an important homeostatic regula-tory organ. The degree to which kidney and conduit abnormalities may affect the whole person ranges from a clinically undetectable change to marked deterioration of the nephron reserves, loss of kidney function, and urine transport abnormalities.

The bladder is a voluntarily controllable urine reservoir that normally permits several hours of urine retention. Bladder dysfunction may be due to

pathologic conditions within or outside the urinary system. Within the urinary system, bladder tumors, stones, and inflammatory lesions may produce uri-nary system impairment.

In women, the urethra is a urinary conduit contain-ing a voluntary sphincter. In men, the urethra pos-sesses a voluntary sphincter and propulsive muscles and is a conduit for urine and seminal ejaculations.

Permanent, surgically created urinary diversions are usually performed to compensate for anatomic losses, following cystectomy to allow for urine out-flow. Diversions are evaluated as a part of, and in conjunction with, the assessment of the involved portion of the urinary tract. When permanent impairment of any segment of the urinary system is evaluated, impairments of all components of the upper and lower tract must be evaluated and com-bined to determine renal system impairment. (See the Combined Values Chart in the Appendix.)

7.2a Interpretation of Urinary Symptoms and Signs

Symptoms and signs of upper urinary tract function impairment may include changes in urination; edema; decreased physical stamina; appetite and weight loss; anemia; uremia; loin, abdominal, or costovertebral angle pain; hematuria; chills and fever; hypertension and its complications; abnormalities in the appearance of the urine or its sediment; and biochemical blood changes. Renal disease, especially in early stages, may be made evident only by laboratory findings.

Symptoms and signs of bladder function impair-ment may include urinary frequency, dysuria, incon-tinence, retention, hematuria, pyuria, passage of urinary calculi, and a suprapubic mass.

Symptoms and signs of urethral function impairment include dysuria, diminished stream, retention, incon-tinence, extraneous or ectopic urinary openings, periurethral masses, and diminished urethral caliber.

As is the case for other chapters, signs and symp-toms can be categorized by frequency, severity, and level of functional loss. Never or occasional signs or symptoms, when present up to 33% of the time, do not generally warrant an impairment rat-ing (unless the ensuing disruption in ADLs is sig-nificant). Frequent signs or symptoms are present between 34% and 66% of the time, and continuous signs and symptoms are present 67% of the time and above (with it understood that this level of precision is impossible to achieve clinically). When present, and in general minimal level of signs or symptoms interfere with ADLs 1% to 10% of the time, mild signs or symptoms interfere with ADLs 11% to 25%

of the time; moderate signs and symptoms affect ADLs 26% to 50% of the time and can have an impact on work and recreational activities. Severe signs or symptoms interfere with ADLs up to 75% of the time, to the point of requiring modification of many routine ADLs (personal, work-related, and recreational). Extreme functional loss occurs when symptoms and signs cannot be controlled by medica-tion and therefore interfere with ADLs up to 100% of the time.

7.2b Description of Clinical Studies

Two clinically useful renal function determinations, serum creatinine and the renal clearance of endog-enous creatinine, may serve as criteria for evaluating upper urinary tract function. The serum creatinine level reflects overall renal function. Under normal hydration conditions, the serum creatinine level should be less than 133 μmol/L (1.5 mg/dL).

The glomerular filtration rate, which measures renal clearance of endogenous creatinine, gives a quantita-tive estimate of the total functioning nephron popu-lation. Because longer periods of urine collection improve the reliability of renal function clearance tests, using 24-hour endogenous creatinine clearance measurements may be desirable. The normal creati-nine clearance ranges are 130 to 200 L/24 h (90 to 139 mL/min) for men and 115 to 180 L/24 h (80 to 125 mL/min) for women.

If there are discrepancies or additional information is needed, additional testing may include metabolic studies, tests of electrolytes or chemicals, urine osmolality, urinalyses, cultures, radiologic investiga-tions, and/or isotope studies.

Parenchymal disfiguration and conduit abnormality assessment may require diagnostic procedures such as biochemical lab tests, cystoscopy, biopsy, arteri-ography, radiography of the urinary tract, computed tomography (CT), or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).

Objective techniques useful in evaluating bladder function include (but are not limited to) cystoscopy, cystography, voiding cystourethrography, cystom-etry, uroflometry, urinalysis, and urine cultures.

Objective techniques useful in evaluating urethral function include (but are not limited to) urethros-copy, urethrography, cystourethrography, endoscopy, and cystometrography.

In general, an objective procedure is described as minimally abnormal if there is an anatomic abnor-mality that leads to no more than a 10% degree of functional organ impairment and is generally

asymptomatic. A mild abnormality does not (or would not be expected to) lead to more than a 11% to 25% degree of functional organ impairment, a mod-erate abnormality would result in a 26% to 50% loss of function (if untreated), a severe abnormality would be accompanied by a 51% to 75% functional loss (if untreated), and an extreme abnormality leads to a greater than 75% loss of organ function (if untreated).

7.3 Upper Urinary Tract

7.3a Criteria for Rating Permanent Impairment due to Upper Urinary Tract Disease

The impairment criteria for evaluating upper urinary tract disease are given in Table 7-2. History is key factor. The creatinine clearance, the most accurate reflection of renal function, is an important crite-rion in each class because it quantifies the degree of upper urinary tract functional impairment. Also of relevance are whether there are intermittent or persistent abnormalities in other diagnostic tests, as well as the magnitude and implications of these abnormalities.

Management of patients with upper urinary tract dysfunction may require treatment with medication or dialysis. This burden of treatment compliance (BOTC) has an impact on the ability to perform ADLs that is additive to that caused by the disease process itself. Indeed, BOTC may be the primary source of functional impairment. The degree of functional impairment due to medications, treat-ment, or procedures is based on the tables in Chapter 10, Endocrine and includes an estimate of the like-lihood and impact of side effects, complications (eg, infection), or recurrent procedures from their use. Refer to BOTC in Appendix B. Renal function deterioration that requires either peritoneal dialysis or hemodialysis will generate severe impairment in the 55% to 75% range, a class 4 impairment (Table 7-2). Successful renal transplantation may result in marked renal function improvement; the impairment based on the clinical implications of having a trans-plant alone is now in the 16% to 32% range, a class 2 impairment. However, transplant recipients require continuous observation and medication, which may add to their impairment. For this reason, depending on the type, dosing frequency, and dosing route of medication, as well as the frequency of anticipated diagnostic testing and procedures, especially if inva-sive, patients may receive a higher rating based on the functional implications of these interventions.

Also, evaluate impairment that is related to com-plications of the disease or therapy, such as cushin-goid changes and osteoporosis, as they arise, and combine the appropriate percentages with the final renal impairment estimate (see the Combined Values Chart in the Appendix).

From a physiologic point of view, the individual with only 1 functioning kidney may have normal over-all renal function because of the efficiency of the remaining kidney.4 However, with only 1 kidney, a normal safety factor is lost. Consider the individual with only 1 functioning kidney as having a 10% whole person impairment because of such an essen-tial organ loss. Combine this percentage with the estimate for any other permanent impairment (see the Combined Values Chart in the Appendix).

CLASS 0 0% Impairment of the Whole Person

EXAMPLE 7-1: UPPER URINARY TRACT DISEASE

Subject: 22-year-old man.

History: Backache, fever, hematuria, headache, and hypertension during an attack of hemolytic strepto-coccal tonsillitis at age 20 years. Evaluation at that time showed urine with red blood cells, red blood cell casts; 2.4 g protein/24 h. Creatinine clearance was 72 L/24 h (50 mL/min). At 6 months the creati-nine clearance was 130 L/24 h (90 mL/min).

Current Symptoms: None.

Physical Exam: Normal.

Clinical Studies: Urinalysis: normal. Creatinine clearance: 158 L/24 h (110 mL/min). Biopsy showed no renal disease.

Diagnosis: Complete recovery from post-streptococcal acute glomerulonephritis.

Impairment Rating: 0% impairment of the whole person.

Comment: Full recovery with no permanent impairment.

CLASS 1 1% to 13% Impairment of the Whole Person

EXAMPLE 7-2: UPPER URINARY TRACT DISEASE

Subject: 40-year-old man.

History: Acute renal colic. Passage of small urinary calculus. Two previous episodes of renal colic. All episodes resolve with spontaneous passage of uri-nary calculi.

Current Symptoms: Occasional flank pain; unlimited physical activity.

Physical Exam: Normal.

Clinical Studies: Normal excretory urograms. Studies show no evidence of metabolic disease. Urine, creatinine clearance, and phenolsulfonphtha-lein study results: within normal limits.

Diagnosis: Recurrent renal calculi.

Impairment Rating: 1% impairment of the whole person. His intermittent symptoms are consistent with class 1, but the current absence of physical and static test findings and the normal renal function warrant moving the impairment 2 grades down from the initial default middle grade of 7% to the lowest grade for the class.

Comment: Class 1 assignment based on the expec-tation that calculi will recur based on the natural history of the disease, leading to occasional renal colic, affecting sexual function and ADLs.

EXAMPLE 7-3: UPPER URINARY TRACT DISEASE

Subject: 45-year-old man.

History: Childhood nephritis; emergency appen-dectomy; appendiceal abscess drainage. Adequate postoperative urine output. Serum creatinine: 248 μmol/L (2.8 mg/dL). Prolonged convalescence. Anemia subsided, and stamina returned to normal. During recovery, is on mild to moderate dietary restrictions.

Current Symptoms: Feels well 12 months after appendectomy and engages in most usual daily activities. Decreased exercise tolerance for competi-tive social activities (eg, basketball).

Physical Exam: Unremarkable except for right lower quadrant scar.

EXAMPLE 7-4: UPPER URINARY TRACT DISEASE

Subject: 52-year-old man.

History: Retroperitoneal fibrosis; left lower ure-ter function severely damaged; ureter surgically reconstructed.

Current Symptoms: Upon discontinuing antibac-terial medication, he has repeated pyelonephritis attacks that disrupt activity.

Physical Exam: Left flank tenderness.

Clinical Studies: Excretory urography: vesico-ureteral reflux with apparently normal left kidney architecture and function. Age-adjusted creatinine clearance: 100L/24h (69 mL/min).

Diagnosis: Active unilateral chronic pyelonephritis secondary to vesicoureteral reflux.

Impairment Rating: 24% impairment of the whole person. The initial impairment rating is in class 2, grade C (24%). The findings on imaging studies are consistent with class 2 disease, but the creatinine clearance is consistent with class 0 disease, leading to an adjustment of the impairment rating downward to 16% WPI.

EXAMPLE 7-5: UPPER URINARY TRACT DISEASE

Subject: 50-year-old woman.

History: Successful operation for parathyroid ade-noma. Periodic pyelonephritis attacks from residual calculi in both kidneys with sporadic passage of stones. Continuous medication consisting of once

daily antibiotic controls urinary tract infections and pyelonephritis attacks.

Current Symptoms: Occasional high fever, chills, and back pain. When she is symptomatic, she is unable to do many of her ADLs.

Physical Exam: Bilateral flank tenderness.

Clinical Studies: Age-adjusted creatinine clearance: stable 65 L/24 h (45 mL/min). Excretory urogra-phy: bilateral pyelocaliceal deformities; kidney size unchanged in 3 years.

Diagnosis: Renal calculi and bilateral chronic pyelonephritis.

Impairment Rating: 24% impairment due to upper urinary tract impairment, as the history, physical examination, and functional renal test results reflect class 2, grade C. Combine urinary tract impairment with parathyroid impairment for impairment of the whole person (see the Combined Values Chart in the Appendix).

Comment: Prevent complications with increased water and fluid intake, and by compliance with daily medication.

EXAMPLE 7-6: UPPER URINARY TRACT DISEASE: IMPAIRMENT RATING

Subject: 28-year-old man.

History: Hemodialysis for marked azotemia and oli-guria from progressive chronic glomerulonephritis. Successful renal transplantation of mother’s kidney; good renal function. Azathioprine and prednisone maintenance treatment; close observation for osteo-porosis development.

Current Symptoms: Asymptomatic.

Physical Exam: Cushingoid features.

Clinical Studies: Creatinine clearance: 108 L/24 h (75 mL/min).

Diagnosis: Functioning renal transplant.

BOTC: 3% impairment points given for the use of prednisone.

Impairment Rating: 24% impairment initially assigned due to having a renal transplant. Adjusted downward to 16% (2 grades) based on the class 1 physical examination and creatinine testing, to which 3% is added for the BOTC, leading to an impairment rating of 19%. Combine any permanent impairment percent related to a complication such as osteoporosis if it develops with the renal impairment estimate (see

the Endocrine System chapter and the Combined Values Chart in the Appendix).

Comment: Reevaluate if secondary infection or other complication develops due to immunosuppres-sive therapy.

CLASS 3 36% to 52% Impairment of the Whole Person

EXAMPLE 7-7: UPPER URINARY TRACT DISEASE

Subject: 48-year-old man.

History: Calculi in minor calices of both kidneys. Multiple endoscopic and open surgical removals of stones. Continuous antibacterial medication once daily.

Current Symptoms: Periodic chills, fever, and back pain. Spends several days per month ill at home.

Physical Exam: Bilateral flank tenderness.

Clinical Studies: Notable diminution of a kidney; bilateral pyelographic architectural changes com-pared with previous surgeries and recurrent pyelone-phritis. Creatinine clearance: 65 L/24 h (45 mL/min). Infected urine.

Diagnosis: Renal calculi with bilateral recurrent pyelonephritis.

Impairment Rating: 44% impairment of the whole person. Class 3 impairment, grade C (44%) based on inability of treatment to completely control sig-nificant symptoms and signs of renal disease. The presence of significant abnormal architecture and infected urine as well as the creatinine clearance level of 45 mL/min are also consistent with class 3 and keep him at this grade.

Comment: Monitor and treat recurrent infections.

EXAMPLE 7-8: UPPER URINARY TRACT DISEASE

Subject: 48-year-old man.

History: Automobile abdominal crush injury leads to hematuria. Patient undergoes left nephrectomy and open reduction, internal fixation (ORIF) for femur fracture. Kidney pathology shows ischemia and juxtaglomerular hypertrophy on histologic examination of left kidney. Blood pressure: 150/90

mm Hg. Hospital bed rest for 1 week; then he was discharged. Other pertinent findings are hyper-tensive retinopathy. Blood pressure 2 weeks later: 240/160 mm Hg, 155/95 mm Hg 6 months later. Creatinine clearance at 6 months: 58 L/24 h (40 mL/min). Receiving 3 antihypertensive medications twice daily and a protein-restricted diet.

Current Symptoms: Severe headaches 16 months after accident.

Physical Exam: Blood pressure: 170/110 mm Hg. Eyegrounds: group 2 changes (Keith-Wagener-Barker classification). Left kidney removed.

Clinical Studies: Creatinine clearance: 30 L/24 h (21 mL/min). Malignant hypertensive changes appar-ent on biopsy specimen of right kidney.

Diagnosis: Bilateral malignant hypertensive vascu-lar kidney disease; status post left nephrectomy.

Impairment Rating: 50% renal impairment. The 44% arteriolar nephrosclerosis impairment due to the inability of treatment to control symptoms and signs, which is adjusted upward to 48% based on the cre-atinine clearance level. This is combined with 10% due to the nephrectomy impairment (Section 7.3), for a urinary system impairment of 53%. Combine this with the appropriate cardiovascular impairment value for hypertension to determine impairment of the whole person (see the Combined Values Chart in the Appendix).

Comment: Monitor renal function; protein restriction.

EXAMPLE 7-9: UPPER URINARY TRACT DISEASE

Subject: 52-year-old woman.

History: Receives intermittent dialysis. Needs help with some everyday activities. No clear nephritis history. Her doctor had placed her on a protein-restricted diet.

Current Symptoms: Chronic fatigue.

Physical Exam: Pale; appears weak.

Clinical Studies: Hemoglobin: 80 g/L (8 g/dL). Serum creatinine level: 0.024; gmmol/L (2.1 mg/dL). Diffuse bilateral glomerulonephritis on renal biopsy. Contracted kidneys and normal pyelocaliceal archi-tecture evident on high-dose excretory urography. Urine culture: negative. Creatinine clearance: 32 L/24 h (age-adjusted creatinine clearance of 38.5 L/24h).

Diagnosis: Chronic glomerulonephritis with renal atrophy.5

Impairment Rating: 48% renal impairment. The 44% initial impairment (class 3) due to continued symptoms and signs is modified upward to 48% based on the class 4 creatinine clearance. This will be combined with the appropriate rating for anemia to determine impairment of the whole person (see the Combined Values Chart in the Appendix). Even with adjusting her creatinine clearance level for her age, the impairment is still class 3 as this is not the key factor.

Comment: Monitor renal function.

EXAMPLE 7-10: UPPER URINARY TRACT DISEASE

Subject: 44-year-old man.

History: Family history of polycystic renal disease. Gross hematuria; protein-restricted diet. Until cur-rent episode, he worked regularly and felt well. Requires moderate dietary restrictions.

Current Symptoms: Has fatigue that sometimes precludes work or participation in many of his usual activities but otherwise is relatively asymptomatic. Does experience periods of sudden flank pain on occasion.

Physical Exam: Normal.

Clinical Studies: Serum creatinine: 707 to 884 μmol/L (8 to 10 mg/dL). Creatinine clearance: 35 L/24 h (24 mL/min). Bilateral deformities charac-teristic of severe, end-stage polycystic renal disease on endoscopy and retrograde urograms.

Diagnosis: Bilateral polycystic renal disease; advanced renal insufficiency.

Impairment Rating: 52% impairment of the whole person. The initial rating is class 3, grade C (44%) due to the presence of significant symptoms and signs, which is modified upward to 52% based on the class 4 clinical findings and creatinine clearance level.

EXAMPLE 7-11: UPPER URINARY TRACT DISEASE

Subject: 25-year-old woman.

History: Severe abruptio placentae. Creatinine clearance: 35 L/24 h (24 mL/min). Bilateral defor-mities characteristic of polycystic renal disease on endoscopy and retrograde urograms. Periodic perito-neal dialysis. Anuria for 49 days, then oliguria, then

increased urine output. Serum creatinine level fell without peritoneal dialysis after 60 days. Performed some ADLs despite severely compromised renal function 12 months after anuria. She is on a low-protein, low-sodium, and low-potassium diet and is receiving medications to treat hypertension.

Current Symptoms: Fatigued; requires daily nap.

Physical Exam: Some skin bronzing change.

Clinical Studies: Percutaneous renal biopsy: renal cortical necrosis. Creatinine clearance: 11.5 L/24 h (8 mL/min).

Diagnosis: Renal cortical necrosis and severe chronic renal failure.

Impairment Rating: 52% impairment of the whole person based on renal disease history. Her need for dialysis is only class 3, even though renal function and the results of static objective testing are both class 4. Therefore, her final genitourinary impair-ment rating is 52%, which should be combined with a rating for her hypertension from the cardiovascular chapter (Chapter 4).

CLASS 4 55% to 75% Impairment of the Whole Person

EXAMPLE 7-12: UPPER URINARY TRACT DISEASE

Subject: 56-year-old woman.

History: Chronic progressive glomerulonephri-tis. Severe anemia, azotemia, and oliguria/anuria. Twice-weekly hemodialysis. Feels well for at most 1 or 2 days after treatment. Needs to maintain a pro-tein and potassium restricted diet.

Current Symptoms: Nausea, lethargy, and edema before hemodialysis.

Physical Exam: Cachetic; bilateral peripheral edema.

Clinical Studies: Hemoglobin 60 g/L (6 g/dL).

Diagnosis: Severe chronic renal failure and refrac-tory anemia.

Impairment Rating: 65% renal impairment of the whole person. A class 4 rating of 65% is based on the need for twice weekly hemodialysis. Her class 4 physical findings and inability for urine production could raise her final impairment to 75% depending on the physician’s judgment. This will be combined with the rating for her anemia.

7.4 Urinary Diversion

7.4a Criteria for Rating Permanent Impairment due to Urinary Diversion Disorders

The impairment criteria for evaluating urinary diver-sion disorders are given in Table 7-3.

EXAMPLE 7-13: 10% IMPAIRMENT DUE TO URETEROILEOSTOMY

Subject: 52-year-old woman.

History: Anterior pelvic exenteration and uretero-ileostomy for cervical carcinoma. No recurrent cancer for 7 years. Calculi removed from both kidneys.

Current Symptoms: Periodic pyelonephritis, even with continual medication.

Physical Exam: Flank tenderness.

Clinical Studies: Pyelonephritis on radiologic studies. Creatinine clearance: 50 L/24 h (20 mL/min).

Diagnosis: Ureteroileostomy, urinary diversion, and chronic bilateral pyelonephritis.

Impairment Rating: 35% impairment due to bilateral pyelonephritis and ureteroilestomy. 7.7 Male Reproductive Organs

The male reproductive organs include the penis, scrotum, testicles, epididymides, spermatic cords, prostate, and seminal vesicles. See the follow-ing sections for impairment percentages for male reproductive organs for 40- to 65-year-old men. Evaluators can, at their discretion, adjust the rat-ing upward (for men younger than 40) or down-ward (for men older than 65) by 10% based on age and the level of premorbid sexual functioning. For example, class 3 penile impairment in a 30-year-old man who was sexually active previously would be rated at 16.5% (15% + 0.1[15%]). New treat-ments, when successful, may decrease the degree of impairment.

7.7a Penis

The penis has the sexual functions of erection and ejaculation. The urinary function of the penis is dis-cussed in the first part of this chapter on the urethra (Section 7.6). Penile functional impairment symp-toms and signs include erection and sensation abnor-malities and partial or complete loss of the penis.

When evaluating penis impairment,10–13 consider both sexual and urinary function impairment. Determine sexual function impairment according to the following classifications. To determine impairment of the whole person, combine this estimate with the appropriate percentage for estimated urinary function impairment. This classification also may be used to estimate penile implant use impairment (see the Combined Values Chart in the Appendix). The ratings for male sexual function are for physical objective loss of function. Loss of libido, interest, or orgasm would be considered under Mental and Behavioral Disorders (Chapter 14) ratings.

Objective techniques useful in evaluating penis func-tion include (but are not limited to) penile tumes-cence studies, Doppler ultrasound penile blood flow evaluations, dynamic cavernosometry and caver-nosography, and angiography.11–15

7.7e Testicles, Epididymides, and Spermatic Cords

The testicles produce spermatozoa and synthesize male steroid hormones. The epididymides and spermatic cords transport the spermatozoa.

Testicular, epididymal, and spermatic cord impair-ment signs and symptoms include local or referred pain; tenderness and change in size, contour, position, and texture; and testicular hormones and seminal fluid abnormalities.

Objective techniques useful in evaluating testicular, epididymal, and spermatic cord function include (but are not limited to) vasography; ultrasound; lymphan-giography; spermatic arteriography and venography; biopsy; semen analysis; and hormone studies for follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), ketosteroids, and hydroxysteroids.

7.7g Prostate and Seminal Vesicles

The prostate and seminal vesicles provide the appropriate nutrition, environment, and transport for spermatozoa and semen. 7.8 Female Reproductive Organs

The female reproductive organs include the vulva, vagina, cervix, uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries. Female reproductive system impairment is influ-enced by age, especially if the woman is of child-bearing age. Consider the physiologic differences between premenopausal and postmenopausal women when evaluating and estimating female reproductive organ impairment.15

7.8a Vulva and Vagina

The vulva has cutaneous, sexual, and urinary func-tions. Urinary function is discussed in the first part of this chapter on the urethra (Section 7.6). The vagina has a sexual function and also serves as a birth passageway. The clitoris is an erectile organ that has an important role in sexual functioning.

Vulval and vaginal function impairment symp-toms and signs include sensation alteration or loss; lubrication loss; partial or complete absence; vulvovaginitis; vulvitis; vaginitis; cicatrization; ulceration; stenosis; atrophy or hypertrophy; neoplasia or dysplasia; difficulties with sexual intercourse, urination, or vaginal delivery; and underlying perineal structure support defects. The ratings for female sexual function are for physical objective loss of function. Loss of libido, interest, or orgasm would be considered under psychological ratings.

7.8c Cervix and Uterus

The cervix serves as a passageway for sperma-tozoa and menstrual blood, maintains closure of the uterus during pregnancy, and serves as a portion of the birth canal during vaginal deliv-ery. Hormones, elaborated by the ovaries or administered exogenously, influence the uterus. The uterus serves as the organ of menstruation, a means of spermatozoa transportation, and the container of fertilization products. The uterus supplies the power for the first and third stages of labor and, in part, for the second stage.

Cervical and uterine functional impairment symp-toms and signs include abnormalities of menstrua-tion, fertility, pregnancy, or labor; excessive cervical canal size, stenosis, or atresia; cervical incompetence during pregnancy; noncyclic hemorrhage; uterine displacement; dysplasia; and neoplasia.

Objective techniques useful in evaluating cervical and uterine function include (but are not limited to) cervi-cal mucous studies; vaginal, cervical, and intrauterine cytologic smears; biopsy; ultrasound; radiologic stud-ies using radiopaque contrast media; blood and urine hormone studies; basal body temperature recordings; sperm concentration, mobility, and viability studies; uterus dilation and curettage; endometrium micro-scopic study; gynecography; laparoscopy; CT; MRI; hysteroscopy; ultrasound placental localization tech-niques; and saline solution sonohysterography.

Symptoms and signs of fallopian tube and ovarian dys-function include pelvic pain, vaginal bleeding or dis-charge; fallopian tube stenosis or obstruction; abnormal morphologic characteristics; pelvic masses; neoplasms; absent, infrequent, or abnormal ovulation; abnormal hormone secretion; and menstrual dysfunction.

Objective techniques useful in evaluating fallopian tube and ovarian function include (but are not lim-ited to) cervical and vaginal cytologic smears; pelvic

roentgenography; hysterosalpingography; gynecog-raphy; ovarian biopsy; blood and urine hormonal assays; ultrasound; CT; MRI; laparoscopy; and basal body temperature studies.
